LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control

LynnReal AI
Technical report, November 16, 2026
Abstract

Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741 ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89 GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

11footnotetext: Contributors and affiliations are listed in Appendix G.

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models are transforming video generation from passive content synthesis into environments that respond to user actions. Early systems such as Genie [1] demonstrated action-controllable generation, while recent advances in Matrix-Game 3.0 [2], PAN [3], and open world models [4, 5, 6, 7] have improved interactivity, temporal consistency, and accessibility. Yet most interaction paradigms remain centered on navigation, camera motion, or high-level instructions. These controls determine where users look or move, but offer limited ability to manipulate the objects they encounter. Enabling such manipulation requires a world model to respond not only to changes in viewpoint, but also to the fine-grained actions through which users interact with their surroundings.

Hands offer a direct and expressive interface for this purpose: reaching, grasping, releasing, and coordinated bimanual movements communicate intentions that are difficult to specify through text or navigation commands. Recent efforts, including HandWorld [8], Hand2World [9], Generated Reality [10], Dexterous World Models [11], and JointControlVideo [12], have begun to connect articulated hand motion with visual generation. However, reliable hand-controlled interaction presents challenges that are distinct from conventional video synthesis. First, hands and their contact regions occupy only a small portion of each frame, so global generative objectives can underemphasize precisely the details that determine control fidelity. Second, accelerating a high-quality video model into a few-step causal generator can amplify local motion errors: the student must preserve articulated interactions while conditioning on its own imperfect history. Finally, even when denoising is accelerated, decoding high-resolution video latents can remain a major obstacle to responsive interaction. These challenges call for a training and inference pipeline that preserves interaction fidelity throughout the transition from full-sequence learning to streaming generation.

We introduce LynnReal-Hand, an open-source hand-controlled video world model developed to address these challenges end to end. At its core is Interaction-Preserving Training (IPT), a supervision strategy that explicitly prioritizes fine-grained interaction fidelity at two critical stages: full-sequence pretraining and causal distribution matching. We first build a dataset of 100K interaction clips with aligned hand trajectories, camera poses, and textual descriptions across diverse real and synthetic scenes. During full-sequence learning, we go beyond global flow matching with hand-aware multilevel supervision: a hand-region latent objective penalizes local reconstruction errors directly, while decoded LPIPS and DINOv2 constraints reinforce perceptual structure and hand appearance. This targeted supervision counteracts the weak contribution of small interaction regions to the global training signal and establishes a stronger teacher for subsequent acceleration.

Building on this pretrained model, we learn a causal flow map [13] that generates each video chunk in only three denoising transitions. Teacher-forced training with clean history provides an efficient initialization, but leaves a mismatch with inference, where each new chunk depends on previously generated content. We therefore refine the causal student on self-generated rollouts using distribution matching [14, 15]. However, global score matching alone does not distinguish the visual evidence needed for interaction dynamics from the evidence needed for scene appearance. To allocate these complementary signals, we formulate region-aware dual-score distillation: a hand-conditioned video teacher and critic guide the entire generated sequence, with higher-noise evaluations emphasizing interaction-related corrections, while a complementary image prior supplies appearance guidance only outside hand regions. This spatial separation is essential because the image prior lacks hand conditions and should not override the specified motion. In this way, IPT addresses complementary failure modes of the two training stages: insufficient hand-local learning during pretraining and degraded interaction fidelity during causal acceleration. For open-ended streaming, a bounded attention window and local temporal-position reset keep the student’s history and positional range finite.

Efficient generation also requires efficient reconstruction. We therefore introduce Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact Transformer decoder that preserves the generator’s native latent interface while compressing attention and feed-forward branches and recovering reconstruction quality through representation and temporal distillation. We evaluate the resulting system with HandBench, covering ten hand-interaction sources, including two held-out sources for out-of-distribution testing. On the main benchmark, LynnReal-Hand-Base achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02; the evaluated LynnReal-Hand-Fast model, trained with video-score distillation but without the image-guidance branch, retains 92.49 MANO Dice with three denoising steps. In a separate optimized 540p streaming evaluation on one H200, Fast reaches 18.03 FPS.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Interaction-scale data and evaluation. We curate 100K hand-interaction clips with temporally aligned hand, camera, and semantic conditions, and establish HandBench to assess control fidelity and visual quality across diverse scenes and held-out settings.

  • •

    Interaction-Preserving Training. We develop a unified supervision perspective spanning hand-aware multilevel learning for full-sequence generation and region-aware score allocation for causal distillation, explicitly addressing how hand-control signals are preserved at both stages.

  • •

    Few-step, open-ended causal generation. We combine causal flow-map learning, refinement on self-generated histories, and bounded-window temporal-position management to support three-step streaming generation without an ever-growing attention cache.

  • •

    Fast, high-fidelity video decoding. We propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, which compresses a pretrained Transformer decoder while retaining its native latent interface and restoring spatial and temporal reconstruction fidelity through targeted distillation.

2 Related Work

2.1 Interactive Video World Models

Video world models use learned visual prediction to make an environment respond to user inputs. Genie [1], Matrix-Game 3.0 [2], and PAN [3] develop action-based interaction and long-horizon simulation. WorldPlay [4] and RELIC [5] study geometric consistency and memory, while LingBot-World [6] and SolarWM [7] advance open training and deployment. BiWM [16] provides an open training framework for bidirectional autoregressive world models. These advances provide a foundation for interactive synthesis. Our focus is the additional control and supervision needed when a user specifies articulated hand motion within the generated scene.

2.2 Hand-Controlled Video Generation

Hand-conditioned generation represents actions using meshes, joints, or other spatial controls. HandWorld [8] jointly models video and hand actions; Hand2World [9] studies hand-driven interaction; and Generated Reality [10] combines hand and camera conditioning. Dexterous World Models [11] grounds interaction in rendered static scenes and hand trajectories, while DexAC [17], P3-WAM [18], and JointControlVideo [12] study complementary structured action representations. DreamDojo [19] and EgoWM [20] further connect action-conditioned prediction with embodied learning. We build on this problem setting and study its full training-to-delivery path. In particular, our method emphasizes local hand supervision, separates temporal and appearance score gradients during causal distillation, and reduces the codec cost. Section 5 compares the available native model paths under their recorded conditions.

2.3 Efficient Generation and Open Recipes

Few-step generation reduces the repeated computation of diffusion sampling. AnyFlow [13] learns finite flow transitions; DMD [14] estimates distribution-matching updates from real and fake scores; and Self-Forcing [15] trains autoregressive generators on their own histories. PackForcing [21] bounds long-video history through partitioned KV caches, compression, and context selection. DuoMatching [22] combines video-joint and image-marginal supervision. For hand control, these objectives must preserve a small, moving interaction region as well as global visual appearance. Our score separation assigns these responsibilities explicitly. We also address the complementary rendering cost: Ultra-Fast-VAE retains the native generator latent interface and reconstructs each completed chunk with narrower attention and feed-forward branches, connecting denoising acceleration to a measured reconstruction–latency trade-off.

3 Methods

LynnReal-Hand aims to synthesize continuous visual interactions conditioned on sequential hand motions. We first formulate this task as conditional video generation and introduce hand-aware supervision to improve the fidelity of fine-grained interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and further refine the model on self-generated trajectories through complementary video and image score distillation. Finally, we introduce Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact decoder that efficiently reconstructs video frames from generated latents to enable real-time interaction.

3.1 Hand-Controlled Video Generation

Given an initial image I0I_{0}, a text instruction cc, captured hand conditions HH, and camera poses PP, we model the conditional video distribution pθ​(X∣𝒞)p_{\theta}(X\mid\mathcal{C}), where 𝒞=(I0,c,H,P)\mathcal{C}=(I_{0},c,H,P). The image establishes scene appearance, the text describes the intended activity, the hand sequence specifies articulation and motion, and the camera poses specify the viewpoint. A fixed encoder maps the target video to latents z=ℰ⁡(X)z=\mathcal{E}(X). Conditional flow matching [23] interpolates between these latents and Gaussian noise:

zσ=(1−σ)​z+σ​ϵ,v⋆=ϵ−z,z_{\sigma}=(1-\sigma)z+\sigma\epsilon,\qquad v^{\star}=\epsilon-z, (1)

where ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and σ∈[0,1]\sigma\in[0,1]. The velocity is defined with respect to increasing σ\sigma, while generation proceeds in the reverse direction, from σ=1\sigma=1 to σ=0\sigma=0. The predictor vθ​(zσ,σ,𝒞)v_{\theta}(z_{\sigma},\sigma;\mathcal{C}) is trained with

ℒFM=𝔼⁡[‖vθ​(zσ,σ,𝒞)−v⋆‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|v_{\theta}(z_{\sigma},\sigma;\mathcal{C})-v^{\star}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (2)

where the expectation is taken over training samples, noise, and noise levels. While this objective captures global scene dynamics, it provides limited supervision for the relatively small hand regions, motivating our hand-aware training strategy.

3.2 Stage I: Hand-Aware Full Sequence Learning

With global flow matching [23] alone, we observe failures in hand-interaction regions, where articulated hands become distorted or collapse into noisy structures. We analyze the loss and gradient contributions of these regions and find that both are weak relative to the rest of the frame. These observations indicate insufficient local supervision and lead us to strengthen it at three levels: latent reconstruction, perceptual similarity, and semantic features. Let MHM_{H} be a hand-region mask aligned with the latent grid and let z^=zσ−σ​vθ​(zσ,σ,𝒞)\widehat{z}=z_{\sigma}-\sigma v_{\theta}(z_{\sigma},\sigma;\mathcal{C}) be the predicted clean latent. We define ℒROI=‖z^−z‖MH2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ROI}}=\|\widehat{z}-z\|_{M_{H}}^{2} and optimize

ℒI=ℒFM+λR​ℒROI+λP​ℒLPIPSH+λD​ℒDINOH.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{I}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}+\lambda_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ROI}}+\lambda_{P}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LPIPS}}^{H}+\lambda_{D}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DINO}}^{H}. (3)

The ROI term constrains the hand latents directly. LPIPS [24] compares decoded hand crops with paired images, while DINOv2 [25] patch features provide a complementary semantic constraint. Both feature networks and the native decoder are frozen, but derivatives through the decoder propagate to the generator within valid hand regions. To balance the magnitudes of the global and local losses, we set λR=5\lambda_{R}=5, λP=0.1\lambda_{P}=0.1, and λD=0.05\lambda_{D}=0.05.

As illustrated in Fig. 2, the pretrained H3 VAE [26] encodes the hand video into latent tokens. We concatenate these with Qwen3-VL [27] caption and first-image embeddings and noisy video tokens as input to the diffusion transformer (DiT) [28], which uses bidirectional attention. Camera poses enter through projective positional encoding (PRoPE) [29]. We train all video-transformer parameters while keeping the condition encoders frozen. The resulting model provides both the initialization for Stage II and the frozen video teacher for Stage III. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

3.3 Stage II: Causal Flow-Map Learning

Stage I yields a bidirectional model whose many denoising evaluations and full sequence attention delay interactive responses. We adapt its weights with LoRA [30] to initialize a few-step causal student for Stage III. AnyFlow [13] reduces model evaluations through finite denoising transitions, while a two-chunk causal window reduces attention per evaluation. For chunk kk, let 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} contain the scene and hand conditions, camera poses, and preceding clean history. The transition from noise level σ\sigma to r<σr<\sigma is

zk,r=zk,σ−(σ−r)​Uθ​(zk,σ,σ,r,𝒞k).z_{k,r}=z_{k,\sigma}-(\sigma-r)U_{\theta}(z_{k,\sigma},\sigma,r;\mathcal{C}_{k}). (4)

Here UθU_{\theta} predicts the average velocity over [r,σ][r,\sigma] and is trained with

ℒAnyFlow=𝔼⁡[‖Uθ+(σ−r)​D^σ​Uθ−v⋆‖M2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AnyFlow}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|U_{\theta}+(\sigma-r)\widehat{D}_{\sigma}U_{\theta}-v^{\star}\|_{M}^{2}\right]. (5)

The stopped finite-difference term D^σ​Uθ\widehat{D}_{\sigma}U_{\theta} estimates the total derivative along the predicted trajectory. The loss reduces to flow matching at r=σr=\sigma; inference composes three transitions. Appendix B gives derivative and sampling details. Both Base and Fast can retain only schedule-specific AdaLN outputs to reduce resident parameter storage (Appendix C.1).

Teacher forcing with clean history.

Figure 2(b) separates two video streams during Stage II training: clean ground-truth chunks 𝒴k\mathcal{Y}_{k} and their noisy counterparts 𝒳k\mathcal{X}_{k}. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the fixed caption/first-image context and independent image anchor, and ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} the hand-condition tokens aligned with chunk kk. Writing 𝒜⁡(Q)\mathcal{A}(Q) for the key groups visible to query group QQ, we use

𝒜⁡(𝒴k)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Y}_{k}) =𝒫∪ℋk∪𝒴k−1∪𝒴k,\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}\cup\mathcal{H}_{k}\cup\mathcal{Y}_{k-1}\cup\mathcal{Y}_{k}, (6)
𝒜⁡(𝒳k)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{X}_{k}) =𝒫∪ℋk∪𝒴k−1∪𝒳k.\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}\cup\mathcal{H}_{k}\cup\mathcal{Y}_{k-1}\cup\mathcal{X}_{k}.

The preceding chunk is omitted for k=0k=0. A noisy query cannot read its paired clean target, another noisy chunk, or a future clean chunk. Prefix queries stay within 𝒫\mathcal{P}: Qwen context queries read only Qwen context, while anchor queries may also read the anchor. Each hand group attends only within itself. These restrictions prevent target information from bypassing the video mask through condition tokens. Visible blocks retain dense spatial and temporal attention; causality is imposed between chunks rather than between tokens inside a chunk. W2 therefore counts the current chunk and one preceding chunk, with no spatial compression of the latter. Clean-history and noisy-target groups can be packed into one training sequence without exposing the same-chunk target. Stage II assigns increasing video positions within each training clip; Stage III uses the bounded local clock below.

3.4 Stage III: Region-Aware Score Distillation

Stage II learns with clean histories, but deployment conditions on generated chunks and accumulates errors. We therefore refine the student on its own causal trajectories [15, 14]. In Figure 2(c), the three-step student uses the same W2 visibility as Stage II, replacing the preceding ground-truth chunk with its completed generated chunk 𝒴^k−1\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{k-1}:

𝒜⁡(𝒳k)=𝒫∪ℋk∪𝒴^k−1∪𝒳k.\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{X}_{k})=\mathcal{P}\cup\mathcal{H}_{k}\cup\widehat{\mathcal{Y}}_{k-1}\cup\mathcal{X}_{k}. (7)

Historical keys and values are detached, so later chunks do not backpropagate through earlier generation. The fixed prefix, current hand condition, and retained video history are cached across the three denoising transitions. After denoising, a clean forward pass commits the completed chunk’s keys and values for subsequent generation; noisy intermediate keys are not used as clean history. On advancing the window, we discard older video chunks and the previous hand-condition group. Training rollout, gradient replay, and deployment use this same student path. Let ZθZ_{\theta} denote the resulting rollout. The video teacher and critic score its corrupted full span bidirectionally with native full-sequence positions, whereas the image branch scores individual frames. Their attention and position rules are distinct from the causal student’s. The two branches combine a hand-conditioned video score for scene dynamics with an image score for appearance [22].

Assigning supervision by region.

The image teacher lacks hand conditions. Following Figure 2, we pull its direction back to video latents, mask out the hand region, and add gvg_{v}:

Local RoPE reset for open-ended inference.

A finite attention window bounds the visible history, but absolute temporal positions would still grow beyond the training range. We therefore reuse a local temporal coordinate system in the Stage III student. For physical chunk index kk, window size WW, and oldest retained chunk ak=max⁡(0,k−W+1)a_{k}=\max(0,k-W+1), let huh_{u} be the temporal position of token uu in the first hand-chunk template and Δ\Delta its chunk span. The hand condition always reuses huh_{u}, while retained video chunk jj receives

pj,u(k)=hu+(j−ak+1)​Δ,ak≤j≤k.p_{j,u}^{(k)}=h_{u}+(j-a_{k}+1)\Delta,\qquad a_{k}\leq j\leq k. (11)

The caption/image prefix keeps fixed coordinates, and the independent anchor stays at the first hand-token time. A full chunk contains five native latent planes corresponding to 17 video frames; in the native temporal coordinate system, Δ=17⋅5/3\Delta=17\cdot 5/3. With W2, advancing from [k−1,k][k-1,k] to [k,k+1][k,k+1] moves retained chunk kk from the second local video slot to the first, while the new chunk takes the second slot.

This reassignment also changes the rotary phase of retained keys. At each transformer layer we cache unrotated keys KjrawK_{j}^{\mathrm{raw}} and reapply rotary positional encoding (RoPE) using the reassigned temporal positions:

K~j(k)=R⁡(pj(k))​Kjraw,\widetilde{K}_{j}^{(k)}=R\!\left(p_{j}^{(k)}\right)K_{j}^{\mathrm{raw}}, (12)

where RR also includes the unchanged spatial rotary factors. Reusing keys already rotated at their old positions would leave history and current queries in inconsistent local coordinates; applying another rotation to them would compound the phase. RoPE does not rotate values. Camera PRoPE continues to use the original physical frame indices and poses, independently of the local temporal reset. The reset is shared by student rollout, replay, and inference; the bidirectional video teacher and critic retain native full-sequence coordinates. Consequently, the live KV cache and temporal coordinate range stay bounded as new hand and camera conditions arrive, enabling open-ended autoregression. This bounds the attention state rather than providing persistent long-term memory.

3.5 Ultra-Fast-VAE: Efficient Video Decoding

Although the preceding stages substantially reduce the number of denoising steps, decoding the generated latents into video frames remains a significant bottleneck for real-time interaction. High-fidelity Transformer-based VAE decoders incur substantial computational overhead, even with recent streaming optimizations [32, 33]. Lightweight CNN alternatives offer lower latency but often sacrifice fine-grained reconstruction quality [34], particularly for articulated hands and manipulated objects. To address this trade-off, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact Transformer decoder that combines representation-preserving architectural compression with targeted reconstruction distillation.

Representation-Preserving Architecture Compression. Our key observation is that reducing computation within the attention and feed-forward branches can be more effective than uniformly shrinking the pretrained decoder. Starting from the H3-compatible LightVAE [35], we retain all 26 Transformer blocks and the 2048-dimensional residual stream, while reducing the number of attention heads from 32 to 8 and the SwiGLU [36] hidden dimension from 8192 to 1536. To identify informative components, we estimate the contribution of each intermediate channel jj using

sj=𝔼[aj2]‖γ⊙W:,j‖22,s_{j}=\mathbb{E}[a_{j}^{2}]\left\|\gamma\odot W_{:,j}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (13)

where aja_{j} denotes the channel activation, W:,jW_{:,j} is its downstream projection weight, and γ\gamma represents the residual scaling factors. Attention heads are ranked by aggregating the importance scores of their constituent channels, while FFN channels are selected individually.

Directly retaining the selected weights, however, cannot fully preserve the original branch outputs. We therefore initialize each compressed output projection by fitting the corresponding full-width branch through ridge regression:

minB,b⁡‖AS​B+𝟏​b⊤−Y‖F2+λ​‖B−B0‖F2+10−6​λ​‖b−b0‖22,\min_{B,b}\left\|A_{S}B+\mathbf{1}b^{\top}-Y\right\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda\left\|B-B_{0}\right\|_{F}^{2}+10^{-6}\lambda\left\|b-b_{0}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (14)

where ASA_{S} contains the selected channel activations, YY denotes the original branch outputs, and (B0,b0)(B_{0},b_{0}) are the corresponding pretrained projection parameters. This initialization preserves the dominant pretrained transformations while substantially reducing the computation of each block. The resulting decoder maintains the native latent interface and reconstructs 17 video frames from five available latents without future context or persistent decoder caches.

Representation Distillation and Temporal Reconstruction. To recover reconstruction quality after compression, we train the compact decoder using complementary representation and reconstruction objectives. Rather than relying solely on output-level supervision, we use frozen full-width attention and FFN branches to guide their compressed counterparts. Given the current student hidden features hℓh_{\ell}, the branch distillation objective is

ℒbranch=∑ℓ,q‖Fℓ,qcompact​(hℓ)−sg⁡[Fℓ,qfull​(hℓ)]‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{branch}}=\sum_{\ell,q}\big\|F_{\ell,q}^{\mathrm{compact}}(h_{\ell})-\operatorname{sg}\left[F_{\ell,q}^{\mathrm{full}}(h_{\ell})\right]\big\|_{2}^{2}, (15)

where qq indexes the attention and FFN branches, and sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. We further supervise late-stage features and reconstructed frames using the pretrained decoder as a frozen teacher.

Beyond spatial fidelity, causal video decoding must preserve motion continuity both within and across generated chunks. Let et=I^t−Ite_{t}=\widehat{I}_{t}-I_{t} denote the normalized reconstruction error at frame tt. We introduce temporal difference and chunk-boundary losses:

ℒΔ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\Delta} =⟨wtΔ​|et−et−1|⟩,\displaystyle=\left\langle w_{t}^{\Delta}|e_{t}-e_{t-1}|\right\rangle, (16)
ℒ∂\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\partial} =⟨wtΔ​|et−et−1|⟩t=17​k,\displaystyle=\left\langle w_{t}^{\Delta}|e_{t}-e_{t-1}|\right\rangle_{t=17k},

where wtΔ=1+2​(mt∨mt−1)w_{t}^{\Delta}=1+2(m_{t}\lor m_{t-1}) emphasizes regions containing hand motion, and mtm_{t} denotes the corresponding hand mask. These objectives penalize discrepancies in temporal changes, particularly at chunk boundaries. The overall training objective combines dense pixel reconstruction, frozen-teacher supervision, and auxiliary losses:

ℒVAE=λp​ℒpix+λt​ℒteacher+∑jλj​ℒj,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}}=\lambda_{p}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pix}}+\lambda_{t}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{teacher}}+\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\mathcal{L}_{j}, (17)

where λp=50\lambda_{p}=50 and λt=10\lambda_{t}=10. The auxiliary terms include branch and feature distillation, temporal reconstruction, and perceptual supervision using LPIPS [24] and DINOv2 [25]. With quantized execution and graph replay, Ultra-Fast-VAE achieves 34.43 dB PSNR with only 361.2M parameters and 46.77 ms decoding latency for 17 frames at 1344×7681344\times 768 on a single H200. Detailed architecture and optimization settings are provided in Appendix E.

3.6 Data Engine Construction

We construct a unified data pipeline for hand- and camera-conditioned egocentric video generation. The pipeline converts heterogeneous videos into interaction clips with temporally aligned 3D hand parameters, hand renderings, camera trajectories, and textual descriptions. It combines visual quality filtering, motion annotation, interaction verification, and diversity-aware sampling to obtain a training corpus of 100K clips.

Video collection and preprocessing.

We collect videos from public egocentric datasets and online sources, supplemented with first-person interaction videos synthesized by MiniMax-H3 [26]. Source videos must have a resolution of at least 720p, a frame rate of at least 24 fps, and more than 200 frames; only egocentric views are retained from multiview recordings. We use OmniShotCut [37] to identify shot boundaries and exclude transition intervals. Within each continuous shot, we extract 125- or 240-frame clips at 24 fps. To provide a sharp conditioning image, we select the starting frame with the highest grayscale Laplacian variance among up to ten valid frames following each candidate cut position. Clips are encoded as H.264 videos with a 768-pixel short side while preserving aspect ratio. We additionally enhance a subset of videos using SparkVSR to improve visual quality. We reject poorly exposed clips using brightness statistics, then retain the top 80% ranked by the overall COVER quality score [38]. PaddleOCR detects persistent subtitles in the lower third of the image. Subtitled landscape clips are discarded; portrait clips are consistently cropped only when subtitle removal requires trimming at most 25% of the image height. All cropping precedes motion annotation.

Hand annotation and detection completion.

We apply the WiLoR hand detector [39] frame by frame, remove duplicate and temporally inconsistent detections, and discard clips with hands detected in fewer than 50% of frames. For retained clips, short gaps bounded by valid same-side detections are filled by interpolating box centers and sizes when the preceding hand is away from the image boundary. Remaining gaps are addressed with SAM 3 [40], prompted with “hand” within an enlarged region around the preceding same-side box. We convert the largest predicted instance into a box, preserve the track’s handedness, and limit consecutive SAM-based completions. After further cleanup and smoothing, clips with hand coverage below 90% are rejected. WiLoR then estimates MANO [41] pose, shape, global orientation, and camera-space translation from the completed boxes. We temporally smooth parameters within valid intervals and render the resulting meshes on a black background, matching the video clip’s frame count, resolution, and frame rate.

Camera annotation.

We estimate camera intrinsics and per-frame poses with ViPE [42], using GeoCalib for intrinsic initialization and MoGe-2 metric depth priors to constrain scale during geometric optimization. To reduce interference from moving hands, we extract binary silhouettes from the hand renderings, apply morphological closing and dilation, and exclude these regions from the geometric constraints. Reusing hand annotations replaces ViPE’s generic foreground detection and segmentation stages. We reject trajectories with missing or invalid poses, inconsistent frame indexing, translation jumps, abrupt rotations, or repeated large direction reversals. Translation steps exceeding five times the local mean, adjacent rotations above 60∘60^{\circ}, and relative rotations above 100∘100^{\circ} within approximately 1.2 seconds trigger rejection.

Semantic annotation and interaction verification.

We use Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [43], deployed with vLLM, to assign background and activity labels and generate interaction descriptions from chronologically ordered frames sampled at 1 Hz, including the first frame. Descriptions establish the initial scene and summarize visible actions and state changes without inventing unobserved events. Camera motion and viewpoint changes are excluded from the text, leaving them to the camera condition. In a separate verification pass, the model examines frames sampled every 25 frames and checks three criteria: an egocentric viewpoint, only the camera wearer’s hands with no other people visible, and purposeful hand–object interaction. We retain only clips that explicitly pass all three checks. Valid interactions include grasping, placing, assembly, tool use, and sustained manipulation; hovering, empty gestures, and static display are excluded.

Training-set selection.

Finally, we sample without replacement using weights proportional to the product of inverse background-label and activity-label frequencies. This increases the selection probability of less frequent environments and actions. Each selected sample contains a video clip, aligned hand parameters and renderings, camera intrinsics and poses, and an interaction caption, providing visual targets and complementary motion and language conditions for generation training.

4 HandBench: Evaluating Hand-Controlled Interaction

4.1 Benchmark Construction

Evaluating hand-controlled video generation requires assessing not only visual realism but also whether the generated interactions faithfully follow the specified hand motions. Existing video quality metrics alone cannot adequately capture such fine-grained control accuracy, particularly for complex hand-object interactions. To enable a more comprehensive evaluation, we construct HandBench, a benchmark that jointly assesses hand-motion fidelity, visual quality, and scene consistency across diverse interaction scenarios.

HandBench comprises 200 video sequences collected from ten sources, with 20 sequences each from EgoDex [44], H2O [45], HOI-4D [46], OpenAoE [47], TACO [48], ARCTIC [49], CaptainCook4D [50], Ego4D [51], EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [52], and synthetic scenes generated by H3 [26]. These sequences encompass diverse interaction patterns, including fine-grained object manipulation, coordinated bimanual actions, tool use, and interactions with articulated or deformable objects. For each sequence, we preserve the original video interval, spatial crop, and temporally aligned hand and camera conditions to ensure consistent reference-based evaluation. We use 160 sequences from eight sources for the main benchmark. H2O and TACO are excluded from world-model training and reserved for out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, with 20 sequences from each source.

4.2 Evaluation Metrics and Protocol

A reliable evaluation of hand-controlled generation must distinguish accurate motion following from visual plausibility, as realistic-looking videos may still deviate substantially from the prescribed hand trajectories. We therefore adopt projected MANO [41] mesh-silhouette Dice as our primary control metric, measuring the spatial agreement between reference hand geometry and hands independently reconstructed from generated frames. This metric evaluates whether the generated hand configurations follow the intended movements while accounting for their projected positions and shapes.

To complement control accuracy, we evaluate reconstruction fidelity using PSNR, SSIM [53], and LPIPS [24], and assess video distribution quality using FVD [54]. We further measure semantic alignment and temporal consistency through weighted CLIP [55] similarity and VBench [56] subject and background consistency metrics. Camera-motion adherence is evaluated using background motion agreement, allowing us to distinguish viewpoint following from hand articulation. Together, these metrics provide complementary assessments of interaction fidelity and visual coherence without reducing them to a single aggregate score. For fair comparison, we preserve each method’s native temporal sampling and align generated frames with their corresponding reference frames. All methods are evaluated on common valid support, with scalar metrics aggregated using equal weights across data sources and FVD computed from pooled video features. Detailed metric definitions and evaluation procedures are provided in Appendix A.

5 Experimental Results

We adapt bidirectional Hand2World [9] on the training corpus and Generated Reality [10] on its ARCTIC subset to reduce domain mismatch; streaming Hand2World and JointControlVideo [12] use released models. Comparisons share 768p cases, native temporal sampling, and source-frame alignment. -Fast uses three transitions with video-score distillation and image guidance disabled. Appendix C specifies model paths.

5.1 Quantitative Results

In Table 1, -Base leads FVD and MANO Dice (93.02) on the eight-source cohort, reducing FVD by 38.3% relative to adapted bidirectional Hand2World. -Fast retains Dice 92.49 with three denoising transitions. -Base also leads the held-out H2O and TACO comparisons with the same models.

Tables 2 and 3 separate generation from reconstruction cost. At 540p, -Fast delivers 17 frames with a mean latency of 0.741 s and throughput of 18.03 FPS, including online hand encoding and decoding. In the separate 768p reconstruction evaluation, Ultra-Fast-VAE reaches 34.43 dB PSNR at 46.77 ms per 17 frames, compared with 30.40 dB at 10.90 ms for Tiny-H3 [34]. Workload-specific protocols appear in Appendices C.3 and E.

User preference. -Base and -Fast are preferred over every baseline (Table 6). Their 70.5%/58.5% preference rates against Hand2World-Bi support the perceptual quality of three-step generation.

5.2 Qualitative Results

Figure 5 compares generation under supplied hand and camera conditions with GT. Figure 5 examines reconstruction detail. An additional demo scene and six-method HandBench comparisons, including Fast, appear in Appendix F.

Everyday interaction through hand motion.

Figure 6 presents selected Base demonstrations organized by the interaction they depict. Fishing, folding cloth, cooking, painting, playing an instrument, and approaching a bird place different demands on hand articulation and local contact. Each generated frame includes its aligned MANO hand condition in a consistent upper-right inset. The translucent WASD and rotation controls inside each generated frame follow the convention in Figure 5 and visualize the supplied camera motion. Generated frames come from the clean videos used in the demo.

Imaginative scenes with the same interface.

Figure 7 extends the presentation to luminous objects, projected layouts, a robotic interface, floating forms, a portal, and freehand lettering. The hand sequence provides a common spatial interface while the surrounding scene and visual response change. The generated videos in both figures use our Base model and illustrate the range of selected demonstrations. Visual selection and input conditions are described in Appendix F.2. Matched comparisons with the six benchmark methods are retained in Appendix F, using the author-selected candidate cases.

5.3 Ablation Study

Complementary hand supervision. The configurations in Table 4 associate stronger hand alignment with lower perceptual error and improved video quality. The full objective exceeds global flow matching alone by 5.72 Dice points. This joint pattern is consistent with the motivation for combining direct latent constraints with decoded perceptual and feature supervision: agreement in latent space benefits from constraints on the appearance it produces.

Causal model refinement. Table 5 compares the Stage-II initializer with the final causal model on all 200 HandBench cases. Both use three denoising transitions. The final model improves FVD from 404.68 to 194.01 and MANO Dice from 89.60 to 92.46.

6 Limitations and Future Work

While LynnReal-Hand demonstrates promising performance in hand-controlled video generation, several directions remain open for further exploration. First, our current causal model operates with a limited temporal context and does not explicitly model long-term memory, which may constrain interaction consistency over extended horizons. Incorporating persistent memory mechanisms could enable more coherent and continuous interactions in long-running virtual environments. Second, we observe that the causal flow-map model learned in Stage II already exhibits promising generation quality within the training sequence lengths, even before subsequent score distillation. This suggests an interesting direction toward directly learning high-quality few-step generators through flow-map objectives, potentially eliminating the need for computationally expensive DMD training. We leave the exploration of these directions to future work.

7 Conclusion

We introduce LynnReal-Hand for continuous visual interaction through natural hand motion. Hand-aware supervision, few-step causal generation, and Ultra-Fast-VAE combine accurate control, high visual fidelity, and efficient decoding. Experiments across diverse interaction scenarios support the effectiveness of this framework.

Appendix A Evaluation Metrics

Alignment and aggregation.

Paired metrics use common original-source frame indices without interpolation. Scalar scores are averaged over videos within each source and then equally across sources; FVD uses pooled video features.

Hand following.

Frozen WiLoR [39] reconstructs hands independently from generated images. Reference and generated MANO [41] meshes are projected into the same output coordinates. For their union masks MtR,MtGM_{t}^{R},M_{t}^{G}, we compute

DMANO=100|𝒯v|​∑t∈𝒯v2​|MtR∩MtG||MtR|+|MtG|,𝒯v={t:|MtR|>0}.D_{\mathrm{MANO}}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{T}_{v}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{v}}\frac{2|M_{t}^{R}\cap M_{t}^{G}|}{|M_{t}^{R}|+|M_{t}^{G}|},\quad\mathcal{T}_{v}=\{t:|M_{t}^{R}|>0\}. (18)

Frames are sampled at 4 Hz on common source indices, without mask dilation or pose alignment. Missing generated hands score zero; frames without reference hands are excluded.

Visual quality and consistency.

PSNR pools pixel MSE within each video before taking the logarithm. PSNR and grayscale SSIM [53] use a centered, aspect-preserving 1344×7681344\times 768 canvas, including black padding. SSIM uses an 11×1111\times 11 Gaussian window (σ=1.5\sigma=1.5), excluding the outer five map pixels. VGG [57] LPIPS [24] averages aligned pairs at 448×256448\times 256 with inputs in [−1,1][-1,1]. FVD [54] compares means and sample covariances of 400-dimensional Kinetics-I3D [58] features from 32 distinct, uniformly spaced frames per video.

For weighted CLIP [55], unit-normalized CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings ut,vt,qu_{t},v_{t},q represent generated frames, aligned reference frames, and the shared caption:

CCLIP=0.2​100T​∑tut⊤​q+0.2​100T−1​∑t=1T−1ut⊤​ut−1+0.6100T∑tut⊤vt.\begin{split}C_{\mathrm{CLIP}}={}&0.2\,\frac{100}{T}\sum_{t}u_{t}^{\top}q+0.2\,\frac{100}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}u_{t}^{\top}u_{t-1}\\ &+0.6\,\frac{100}{T}\sum_{t}u_{t}^{\top}v_{t}.\end{split} (19)

Aligned 640×360640\times 360 images pass through the frozen 224-pixel center-crop processor; cosines are not clipped. VBench [56] SC/BC use DINO [59] ViT-B/16 and CLIP ViT-B/32, respectively, averaging nonnegative cosine similarity to the first and preceding frames on the 0–100 scale.

Camera following.

Cam-BG compares background motion at 4 Hz and 640×360640\times 360. Hand-condition silhouettes are masked using their adjacent-frame convex hull with 31×3131\times 31 dilation; the 12-pixel border and reference padding are excluded. Shi–Tomasi/LK tracks with at most one-pixel forward–backward error fit RANSAC homographies. Valid fits require 40 tracks, 24 inliers, 60% inliers, and three-quadrant support.

For reference/generated displacements a,ba,b, let cc be their nonnegative directional cosine and rr the smaller ratio of their norms, with denominators clamped at 10−810^{-8}. With τ=0.5\tau=0.5 pixels, grid-point agreement is

A⁡(a,b)={c⁡(a,b)​r​(a,b),‖a‖≥τ,exp⁡[−(‖b‖/τ)2],‖a‖<τ.A(a,b)=\begin{cases}c(a,b)r(a,b),&\|a\|\geq\tau,\\ \exp[-(\|b\|/\tau)^{2}],&\|a\|<\tau.\end{cases} (20)

Pair scores average 100​A100A over supported points; video scores average eligible pairs. Generated-estimation failures score zero on reference-observable pairs. All methods use common support with at least 25% observable reference pairs per video.

Appendix B Training and Implementation Details

B.1 Stage-I Implementation

The full 33B transformer is optimized in BF16 with frozen condition encoders and FlashAttention-3 [60]. Qwen encodes only the first image and caption; the native H3 VAE encodes the hand video. Native hand and target planes contain 24×4224\times 42 tokens with 1×2×21\times 2\times 2 patches. Camera conditions use fixed intrinsics and first-relative extrinsics. H3’s data-directed prediction has the opposite sign to the noise-directed velocity in the main text, with t=1−σt=1-\sigma.

All target planes are noised and supervised. Anchor and hand tensors use 0.999​X+0.001​ϵ0.999X+0.001\epsilon with time label 0.999. Hand perceptual supervision samples a 16×1616\times 16 latent crop, decodes five predicted latents with two detached context latents, and evaluates LPIPS and DINOv2 on the corresponding 256×256256\times 256 hand region. The ROI margin is 0.2.

B.2 Stage-II Implementation

Stage II trains rank-384 LoRA [30] and interval-conditioning parameters (2.08B trainable parameters). FP32 AdamW uses (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95), cosine decay, and EMA 0.999; CFG is disabled.

For the derivative term in Eq. 5, let d=sg⁡(vθ)d=\operatorname{sg}(v_{\theta}), σ−=max⁡(r,σ−h)\sigma_{-}=\max(r,\sigma-h), and σ+=min⁡(1,σ+h)\sigma_{+}=\min(1,\sigma+h). We use

D^σ​U\displaystyle\widehat{D}_{\sigma}U =sg⁡[U+−U−σ+−σ−],\displaystyle=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\frac{U_{+}-U_{-}}{\sigma_{+}-\sigma_{-}}\right], (21)
U±\displaystyle U_{\pm} =Uθ​(z+(σ±−σ)​d,σ±,r).\displaystyle=U_{\theta}(z+(\sigma_{\pm}-\sigma)d,\sigma_{\pm},r).

Target evaluations share conditions and are detached; only the interval prediction receives gradients. Interior time pairs apply the same monotone shift to uu and v​uvu, for independent uniform u,vu,v. Stopped loss balancing scales the interval objective relative to the diagonal reference.

B.3 Stage-III Score Distillation

The image bridge maps five 24-channel H3 planes through a width-256 projection, eight spatial residual blocks, and 2×2\times pixel-shuffle upsampling. Physical-offset embeddings select the corresponding frame. The bridge is frozen after fitting, while its input derivative remains active. Four temporal locations supply image supervision. Qwen-Image [31] uses CFG4 and native norm rescaling without hand or camera conditions; a Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [61] critic fits one-frame image latents. After the bridge VJP, image gradients are zeroed inside the hand ROI.

The dual-score configuration uses video CFG3, shift-3 student rollout, and shift-12 video-score noise. The negative branch retains image and camera conditions while omitting hand and text conditions. Critics receive five optimizer updates per generator update after 10 warmup updates; the image weight ramps from 0.001 to 0.1 during warmup. Student EMA is 0.999. Earlier generated histories are detached when replaying trainable rollout exits.

The evaluated Fast model uses video-score training with uniform noise, paired hand supervision, and a non-hand adversarial term; its image-score branch and image critic are disabled.

Appendix C Inference and Runtime

C.1 Evaluated Model Paths

LynnReal-Hand-Base uses joint CFG3 and the native H3 VAE at 1344×7681344\times 768. Its 30-point shift-3 schedule performs 29 Euler updates with two evaluations per update. Fast uses three shift-3 flow-map transitions, W2 history, native H3 anchor encoding, Tiny-H3 [34] hand encoding, and FP16 Ultra-Fast-VAE for quality evaluation. The same Fast model supplies the pairwise preference results.

Streaming Hand2World [9] and JointControlVideo [12] use released models. Bidirectional Hand2World adapts rank-256 attention LoRA and its camera adapter on the adaptation corpus (84,305 examples; 32,000 sample visits), retaining 50 native sampling steps, CFG1, and the full Wan VAE without TeaCache [62]. Generated Reality [10] adapts rank-32 LoRA and a motion encoder in the official 5B model on 1,146 ARCTIC clips from subjects s01–s09, reserving s10 for reproduction validation. All methods retain native source-frame alignment without frame repetition or playback changes.

Schedule-specific AdaLN storage.

For both LynnReal-Hand-Base and LynnReal-Hand-Fast, per-block AdaLN modulation depends only on the prescribed time conditions. A fixed sampling schedule therefore needs only the modulation values at its visited times and clean-conditioning boundaries; Fast uses the corresponding start/end-time pairs. The inference export stores these values directly and omits the learned block projection matrices, avoiding their loading and device residency. The default Base and three-step Fast tables occupy 535.3 and 55.4 MiB, respectively. This storage specialization leaves the sampling rule unchanged; total memory also includes activations, codecs, KV caches, and graph buffers.

C.2 Timing Boundaries and Hardware

Table 2 reports single-H200 measurements. Baseline and Base rows use their available support from the original 140-clip timing cohort; different case support and resolutions preclude a controlled speed ranking. Offline latency measures the full sequence. Streaming Hand2World reports native four-frame latency and post-anchor throughput. Comparison encoding is excluded. Base retains cached conditions and transformer/VAE device swaps with the native decoder; its peak uses the original full AdaLN projections.

C.3 Optimized Streaming Deployment

The accelerated Fast path combines quantized projections, fused operators, condition caches, full 50-block DiT compilation, CUDA graphs, and W8A8 Ultra-Fast-VAE on one H200. Native 960×544960\times 544 computation is vertically cropped to 960×540960\times 540 output. Three transitions and W2 history are retained.

One warmup rollout and three measured repeats on the 124-frame example give 15 steady full chunks, yielding 18.0295 FPS and mean latency 740.69 ms. Latency starts with available hand/camera conditions and ends when synchronized frames reach host memory; it includes online hand encoding, prefill, generation, and decoding. Continuous FPS additionally includes the preceding clean KV commit. Loading, initial-image conditioning, cold compilation, warmup, video encoding, acquisition, and display are excluded. The Fast peak in Table 2 comes from a separate measurement of the released sampling-specialized model on the same 124-frame input geometry. After one full warmup and release of unused allocator cache, three rollouts reach 34.89 GiB maximum PyTorch-allocated device memory. Conditions are prepared in advance, with the native H3 VAE and Qwen encoder off device during generation. The peak includes the quantized transformer, online hand encoder, Ultra-Fast-VAE, KV caches, and graph buffers; cold loading and conditioning preparation are excluded. Timing and the 768p quality evaluation use separate model weights and protocols.

Appendix D Additional Generator Analyses

D.1 Score-Direction Diagnostics

Figure 3 uses video noise levels 0.25 and 0.90 and mapped image noise 0.638. Teacher/critic CFG is 3/1 for video and 4/1 for images. The guided view decodes the unit step x−(Df−Dr)x-(D_{f}-D_{r}) before DMD normalization; the image probe also precedes bridge pullback and hand masking. Heatmaps show channel-RMS prediction differences with a fixed 99th-percentile scale per branch. The probes visualize score responses rather than optimizer updates; their magnitudes are not comparable across latent spaces.

Appendix E Ultra-Fast-VAE: Architecture, Training, and Evaluation

E.1 Decoder Architecture

Figure 8 summarizes width compression, projection initialization, and reconstruction distillation.

Architecture and causal interface.

The decoder retains 26 blocks and a 2048-channel residual stream, with eight 64-dimensional attention heads and 1536-channel SwiGLU branches. It has 361.217M parameters. As in the H3-compatible LightVAE [35], 28 overlapping 16×1616\times 16 latent tiles are blended spatially. Each tile processes the five current latents using the seven-position reference RoPE clock; the readout crops 20 native positions to 17 video frames. Attention is joint within a chunk and causal between chunks, with no future latents or decoder history cache.

E.2 Training and Export

Initialization and supervision.

Energy-ranked heads/channels and ridge-fitted output projections initialize the reduced branches, as defined in Section 3.5. Reconstruction fine-tuning updates the student decoder while frozen full-width branches provide detached local and feature targets. Neither the teacher branches nor the image bridge appears in the deployed decoder.

Training uses native-H3 latents and original frames from 100,722 videos across 12 sources. A disjoint 1,394-video pool is excluded from fitting and calibration; 200 stratified videos from it select the export. Each update accumulates two videos, each with two consecutive 17-frame chunks. Dense MSE supervises all pixels; sampled spatial and perceptual losses emphasize hand appearance. Temporal and boundary losses match changes in reconstruction error across adjacent frames, including chunk transitions. Table 7 lists coefficients. LPIPS [24] and DINOv2 [25] provide frozen perceptual features; the loss families build on LynnReal-Omni [35].

Optimization and export.

FP32 AdamW uses (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.99)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.99), zero weight decay, gradient clipping at 1, and learning rates 10−510^{-5} for attention/FFN and 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} for other parameters. Export averages six late-training parameter states. Input-channel smoothing [63] with α=0.75\alpha=0.75 and the folded color affine are calibrated on training videos only; validation frames do not supply fitting targets.

W8A8 projections use per-token activation and per-row weight scales with INT32 accumulation and FP16 output. FlashAttention-3 [60], fused RMSNorm/RoPE/SwiGLU/residual operations, static compilation, and CUDA graphs reduce execution cost. Frame packing and synchronized host transfer are included in measured decoding latency.

E.3 Reconstruction Evaluation and Timing

Cohort and metrics.

All decoders reconstruct the same native-H3 caches from 200 source-stratified validation videos, comprising 29,818 frames across 12 sources and distinct from HandBench. We score complete five-latent/17-frame chunks against original images at 1344×7681344\times 768, before file compression.

Reconstruction PSNR pools squared error over all frames before the logarithm, unlike the source-macro HandBench PSNR. Temporal deltaMAE averages |et−et−1||e_{t}-e_{t-1}| for normalized reconstruction error et=(I^t−It)/255e_{t}=(\widehat{I}_{t}-I_{t})/255; boundary deltaMAE restricts pairs to chunk transitions. No pair crosses videos. VGG LPIPS samples positions 0, 8, and 16 per chunk at 448×256448\times 256 and averages equally over videos.

Temporal inputs and timing.

Table 8 distinguishes available context from execution cost. Native H3 (SolarRenderer [64]) and LightVAE consume two future latents; StreamRender’s pair schedule [32] may require one. The current-five LightVAE diagnostic changes both lookahead and overlap blending, so it is not an isolated lookahead ablation. StreamRender’s H200 implementation ports its attention call to FA3 while retaining fused operators and graph execution.

Timing uses one H200 and 501 distinct chunks after warmup, discarding the first two chunks after stream reset. Median latency includes decoding, stitching, host transfer, and synchronization, excluding encoding, generation, file operations, cold startup, and future-latent arrival. Throughput divides emitted frames by total decoding time.

Decoder Publication / extra latents Retained decoder history Spatial execution Tiny-H3 (both weights) Current five / 0 Recompute two raw latent positions Native CNN upsampling SolarRenderer / H3 Native stride five / 2 Five overlapping video frames 28 overlapping native tiles SolarX H3 Streaming One latent / 0 Seven-slot KV window, shared-slot recomputation Native tile geometry StreamRender-H3 single One latent / 0 Four rolling KV positions Shifted local windows StreamRender-H3 pair Two latents / at most 1 Four rolling KV positions and pending video frames Shifted local windows LightVAE native Native stride five / 2 Five overlapping video frames 28 overlapping native tiles LightVAE current-five control Current five / 0 None 28 overlapping native tiles Ultra-Fast-VAE Current five / 0 None 28 overlapping native tiles

Precision and visual comparisons.

The same exported weights reach 34.4502 dB in FP16 versus 34.4288 dB in W8A8, a 0.0214 dB difference that includes fusion and rounding effects. Current-five LightVAE reaches 34.9024 dB, while its native input budget reaches 35.1307 dB. These settings are reported separately.

Figure 5 shows matched crops from five videos, with PSNR evaluated on the displayed regions. Figure 9 provides the corresponding full frames. Native H3 uses BF16, Tiny-H3 and LightVAE use FP16, and ours uses W8A8. The blender scene uses archived full-sequence Native H3 decoding and a CPU FP16 LightVAE reference whose full-clip PSNR matches the frozen GPU result within 0.02 dB. Other rows use frozen native-resolution outputs. Display scaling preserves aspect ratios without enhancement; the 200-video benchmark and timing results are unchanged.

E.4 Qualitative Reconstructions

Appendix F Qualitative Generation Comparisons

F.1 Selection and Alignment

HandBench panels are curated from the authors’ 53-case visual-selection pool; quantitative evaluation retains all 200 cases. Six distinct source times are aligned across the saved outputs. Full native viewports are uniformly scaled with padding when needed, with common source-frame alignment. Base, Fast, and adapted baselines match Table 1. Images are not enhanced or temporally interpolated. Display images are compressed uniformly; metrics use the original outputs.

F.2 Demo Showcase Sources

Figures 6 and 7 use twelve curated Base demonstration sequences with joint CFG3 at native 1344×7681344\times 768 and 24 fps. Four existing frames per sequence are shown without image enhancement or temporal interpolation. In Figure 6, hand conditions appear in upper-right insets, and the same translucent WASD/rotation controls used in the comparisons show the supplied camera motion. Pose interpolation is used only for these controls; Figure 7 shows generated frames alone. These examples are separate from HandBench.

F.3 Additional Comparison Examples

Figure 5 shows seedling transplanting and pour-over coffee from the synthetic HandBench subset at four common source times (0.50, 3.125, 6.25, and 8.875 s). Figure 10 provides a separate holographic-keyboard demonstration. GT is the source video; hand conditions and translucent camera controls visualize the inputs. Pose interpolation affects only the controls, not video frames.

Base uses joint CFG3; Fast uses three shift-3 transitions, W2 history, Tiny-H3 hand encoding, and FP16 Ultra-Fast-VAE. Baselines retain their native interfaces and samplers. The keyboard demonstration is separate from the benchmark cohort. Inference durations for these visual examples are excluded from timing tables.
